meta.dataset_label: Vocal Register and Singing Voices in Popular Music (Pudding, Aug 2019)

det_01.label: Origin: The Pudding 'Are Men Singing Higher in Pop Music?' (Aug 2019)
det_01.content: This dataset accompanies The Pudding's August 2019 essay 'Are Men Singing Higher in Pop Music?' by Matt Daniels. The piece used Pandora's vocal-register score — a 1-to-10 scale produced by the Music Genome Project's musicologists — joined to roughly 60 years of Billboard Hot 100 chart data (1958-2019). The published archive contains four CSVs: songs.csv (one row per Hot 100 song with male vocals, 1958-2019, n=11,944), 2019.csv (the 248 charting songs from 2019 narrowed to 80 male-led tracks, with gender, genre, and a 'spoken' flag for rap/hip-hop), avg.csv (yearly mean register across all charting male-led songs), and avg_top.csv (yearly mean register restricted to top-10 hits). Daniels worked with Estelle Caswell at Vox's Earworm series, whose companion video 'We Measured Pop Music's Falsetto Obsession' aired the same month and reached the Webby Awards.

det_02.label: How Pandora's vocal-register score is built
det_02.content: Pandora's Music Genome Project codes each song along ~450 attributes that human musicologists score after listening for 20-30 minutes. Vocal characteristics include the lead vocalist's gender, timbre, breathiness, gruffness, and whether the voice sits in a high or low register. The 'register' value used in this dataset is one of those attributes — a hand-coded 1-to-10 scale where 1 is a deep chest voice (Daniels cites Barry White-style examples as roughly a 2) and 10 is a near-the-top performance like Ginuwine's 'Pony', which scored a 10/10. The scale collapses head voice and chest voice into a single perceived-pitch axis; it does not directly measure falsetto, which is a vocal mechanism rather than a pitch height. That distinction matters: a song can be high in register without being falsetto, and a falsetto passage can sit in a moderate register if it follows a higher belted passage.

det_03.label: Falsetto vs. register: why the distinction matters
det_03.content: Falsetto is a vocal mechanism produced by vibration of the ligamentous edges of the vocal folds, sitting just above the modal (chest) register and overlapping with it by roughly an octave. Male singers historically used falsetto for high notes, while women generally use head voice. The technique was foundational before women sang in choirs and was revived in 20th-century pop by Smokey Robinson, Frankie Valli, the Bee Gees, Prince, and many others. By the late 2010s, critics noted falsetto had become a clear trend among male pop stars including Justin Bieber, The Weeknd, Bruno Mars, Drake, Charlie Puth, Shawn Mendes, Adam Levine, and Sam Smith. In the dataset, however, 'register' is a perceived-height score, so a high register reading captures both high belts and falsetto without separating them.

det_04.label: Headline finding: 2019 top-10 register hit a 60-year high
det_04.content: Daniels's central claim is that, looking only at top-10 Billboard hits with male vocal leads, 2019 was the highest-register year in the dataset's 60-year window. Four of the five top-10 male-led hits that year sat in high register, including Khalid's 'Talk' (which peaked at #3 on the Hot 100 and ranked #8 on Billboard's 2019 year-end chart). The all-songs average for 2019 was 5.95, lower than the '70s and '80s peaks; the top-10 average tells a different story — the very biggest songs are now sung high, even though the average male-led charting song is not particularly high. The previous register peak in the all-songs series was 1988 (Guns N' Roses, Aerosmith, Poison, hair-metal high belts). Another high earlier era was 1977-78, the Saturday Night Fever years, anchored by the Bee Gees' falsetto-led 'Stayin' Alive' (#1 for four weeks).

det_05.label: Why a reader should care: the radio sound of the 2010s changed
det_05.content: The dataset matters because it makes audible something most listeners felt but rarely measured: by the late 2010s the dominant texture of a hit pop song with a male voice had shifted from belted chest-voice rock or croon-style baritone toward a softer, higher, often-falsetto delivery. The Vox Earworm video built on Daniels's data argues that male falsetto became 'nearly impossible to turn on the radio and not hear', tying the trend to streaming-era pop, the rise of the bedroom-pop and post-Drake R&B aesthetic, and EDM's preference for high vocal hooks layered over electronic beats. Independent of cause, the rendering of the chart year by year is the cleanest available picture of a stylistic shift that shaped a decade of radio.

det_06.label: Genre and gender slicing in 2019.csv
det_06.content: The 2019 slice (2019.csv) keeps only the 80 male-led entries from the year's 248 charting Hot 100 songs after dropping primarily spoken/rapped tracks. Each row carries: register (1-10 integer), gender (male, with one row tagged otherwise in error — the analyst should check), genre (Country, Pop, Rap/Hip hop, Rock/Alternative, R&B/Soul, EDM, etc.), and a 'spoken' flag (1 if dominantly rapped, else null). This means the song-level analyses can ask which genre delivered the highest registers in 2019, whether rap/hip-hop's 'spoken' songs cluster at lower registers, and whether the year's outliers come from a specific lane.

det_07.label: Caveat: register is hand-coded, not measured in Hz
det_07.content: Pandora's register score is the result of a human musicologist judging perceived vocal height; it is not an automatic acoustic measurement of fundamental frequency. That has two consequences for analysis. First, scores between adjacent songs may be correlated by rater rather than by actual pitch (rater drift, era effects, label fatigue). Second, a single integer-valued 1-10 axis cannot distinguish between a baritone belting an A4 and a tenor sliding into falsetto on an A4 — they may both score 7 even though the technique differs. Trends across years are still meaningful because the rating standard is held roughly constant by Pandora's editorial team, but readers should treat each song's register as an ordinal rank, not a precise pitch.

det_08.label: Benchmarks for context
det_08.content: Useful external benchmarks the analyst should keep at hand. The 1-10 scale's anchors as Daniels uses them: ~2 = baritone belt or croon (e.g., Barry White), ~5 = mid-range tenor (most baseline pop), ~7 = noticeably high belt, 10 = near-the-ceiling delivery (Ginuwine's 'Pony'). Billboard Hot 100 has been the canonical US singles chart since 1958, so the dataset's first year (1958) is the chart's first year. Saturday Night Fever's release at the end of 1977 produced one of the genre's most famous mass-market falsetto eras, and 'Stayin' Alive' staying at #1 for four weeks in early 1978 is a useful real-world anchor for what a high-register-dominant year sounds like.
